title: The Necessity of Faith and the Example of Noah
english: I believe that because they have overstepped bounds in such a contemptuous and unworthy manner, they will not be granted a second honor of the Spirit, the first having been set aside; rather, it is fitting that they undergo punishments.

For it is not so that "their unfaithfulness will nullify the faith of God" (Rom 3:3), nor, since some have gone about treating it with contempt, shall we record the uncertain nature of divine grace as being lost.

Rather, the Judge of all things will not refuse to let those who have been shaken into such impiety undergo punishments, seeing as they have trampled upon the Son of God and insulted the Spirit of grace, in whom they were sanctified and became partakers of the divine nature.
This [judgment] carries a great recompense.

This is because, through endurance, we must not be satisfied with the exceptional things granted to the perfected, but must always be thirsty, possessing an insatiable state and an unceasing desire for every good thing. We must accumulate for ourselves a good reputation through our actions, maintaining such dispositions as those who love wealth possess, concerning whom it is written, "He who loves silver will not be satisfied with silver" (Eccl 5:10). If those earthly, temporary, and fleeting things do not satisfy them, how much more necessary is it for us to employ more ardent desires, so that we may gain those things from God which extend into infinite ages and possess an ungraspable joy? By faith we understand that the ages were prepared by the word of God, so that the things seen did not come from the things appearing (Heb 11:3).
Faith is, therefore, a truly great and exceptional good.
For it is a wealth that puts away sins and a cleansing from every defilement.

Furthermore, there is a reminder of that which comes from God; it is a path toward sanctification and sonship, and serves altogether as a reminder of every good thing. In this way, the fathers became well-pleasing, and they possessed a glory that is both bright and unsung.
Many have endured even his death, putting on the unfading crown of glory.
Noah, having been charged by faith concerning things not yet seen, stepped forward in piety and was constructing an ark for the salvation of his household.

Because the whole earth had destroyed its way, as it is written, and the heart of man has inclined toward evil from youth, God sent a flood upon all the earth. It was like a garden that had been plundered and watered, yet preserved a noble plant within it—the most excellent Noah—so that the human race might be transformed into a new beginning and be saved upon the earth once more.

Thus, Noah, having been charged by faith, constructed the ark for the salvation of his house, 'into which a few, that is to say, eight souls were saved through water.' For a decree of death has gone out against all those upon the earth, as they were clearly filled with sin, calling down the Creator into irretrievable wrath.
But Noah, being righteous, was being saved universally.

For he believed in God, who commanded the construction of the ark; and while the whole earth was baptized, it was carried along by the waters, taking as its pilot God, the Savior of all. And there was in...

title: Faith and Obedience
english: A remnant of humanity is left to women and children, while the one who has faith has something to boast about.
Abraham, who had faith, offered his son Isaac when he was being tested, and this is a great wonder that I am unable to depart from.
The blessed Abraham, an old man who was childless, sought an heir from God, and after receiving Isaac, he was commanded to sacrifice him.

Abraham's faith was so strong that he overcame the storm of testing, and this is a testament to the stability and safety of holy thoughts, as the most law-abiding Paul will teach, saying Abraham offered Isaac when being tested, having calculated that God is able to raise even from the dead (Hebrews 11:19).
Oh, the stability of faith; oh, the safety of holy thoughts; he gave to God the power to accomplish all.
Abraham believed God and it was reckoned to him as righteousness (Genesis 15:6), for he endured the cross, despising shame, instead of the joy set before him.

He emptied himself, sitting among us, so that, having overcome death in the flesh, then, having conquered it through the resurrection from the dead, he would declare to us that it is possible to return to life.

As the Son of God, he voluntarily took on the most dishonorable and inglorious death, without sparing himself from it, but through his resurrection, he was glorified and abolished the shame and ugliness of his humiliation.
The Son's glory is undeniable, and his resurrection has overcome corruption and abolished shame, declaring to us that it is possible to return to life.

Daniel writes that the Ancient of Days sits on a throne, with a thousand thousands of those ordained for service and ten thousand times ten thousand of those who attend, standing around him (Daniel 7:9-10).
Isaiah also saw the Son in glory, saying 'I saw the Lord Sabaoth sitting on a high throne, and the house was full of his glory, and Seraphim stood around him' (Isaiah 6:1-3).
Christ sat at the right hand of the throne of God.
The scripture teaches that Abraham's faith led him to a great end, for it is written, 'He believed God and it was reckoned to him as righteousness' (Genesis 15:6).

title: Divine Dominion
english: The Son's glory is equal to the Father's, and he shares in the dominion of the highest throne.
The heavenly powers are arranged in a circle around him, and the measure of servitude of created beings is a witness to his glory.

As the Lord sits at the right hand of the Father, he seems to be elevated to the beginnings of such manifest and transcendent glory through the flesh and the economy with the flesh, not having acted humanly, not even because he became flesh.
He hears the words 'Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool' (Psalm 110:1), and whatever the divine nature would subdue, this is borne by the feet of our Savior.

The lowly aspect of humanity is elevated to the dignity of the highest nature, and the Only-begotten Word of God, having established himself in the throne of divinity with flesh, dominates all things not without the Father.
For all things are through both equally, the Father acting and having the energy and will in the Spirit through the Son and with him.
Paul now recalls the story of God's appearance on Mount Sinai, where the Lord dwelled in a fiery manifestation, and the sound of the trumpet was incredibly loud.
The vision was untouchable to the onlookers, and the sound of the trumpet was unbearable.
However, Paul now reminds us that God has promised to shake not only the earth but also the heaven.
This is a reference to the mysterious and renowned event that has been known to both heaven and earth.
There have been two visible changes in the course of human history: one from idolatry to the law, and the other from the law to the gospel.
We are now announcing a third earthquake, a transfer from this world to the next, which will be unshakeable and unmovable.
Therefore, as we receive an unshakeable kingdom, let us have gratitude.
I would gladly ask those who think the kingdom of Christ has been destroyed: whose kingdom does the apostle now remember?
He says it will be shaken and yet always possesses the unshakeable.
